meta.name: Kidney Stone — Severe Flank Pain with Hydromorphone Titration

patient.name: Renata Ford
patient.chiefComplaint: Severe left flank pain, writhing and unable to find a comfortable position

history.hpi: Sudden onset of severe left-sided flank pain approximately 45 minutes ago while at work, described as sharp and colicky, radiating toward the groin. Pain is constant with waves of increased intensity. Associated nausea with two episodes of vomiting. No fever. Reports one prior kidney stone 3 years ago that passed without intervention.
history.lastOralIntake: Coffee and a granola bar approximately 3 hours ago
history.events: Coworkers called 911 after finding her doubled over and unable to sit still in the breakroom

scene.location: Office breakroom, patient found on the floor unable to hold still
scene.bystanders: Two coworkers present, confirm sudden onset with no trauma
visualCues: Patient writhing on the floor, unable to find a comfortable position
Emesis basin with small amount of vomitus nearby
Patient periodically doubling over with waves of pain

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 45-year-old female writhing on the floor, unable to sit still, holding her left flank. She is alert, diaphoretic, and reports 10/10 colicky pain with associated nausea.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, speaking in full sentences between waves of pain
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, strong and rapid
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Intact in all extremities; constantly shifting position due to pain
otherFindings: 10/10 left flank pain, colicky, radiating to groin
Unable to remain still, pacing/writhing behavior
Left costovertebral angle tenderness to percussion
Mild nausea, one episode of emesis prior to EMS arrival
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "It comes in waves — right now it's a 10, please help me, I can't sit still."

transitions.condition: Crew obtains vital signs, assesses pain on a numeric scale, establishes IV access, and administers weight-based hydromorphone with an antiemetic per protocol.

phases.name: Pain assessed and hydromorphone given
phases.description: Crew obtains a full set of vitals, assesses pain using a numeric rating scale, establishes IV access, and administers weight-based hydromorphone along with ondansetron for nausea. Patient is placed in a position of comfort.
phases.triggerCondition: After confirming no signs of shock, AAA, or other life-threatening cause, the crew recognizes classic kidney stone presentation, establishes IV access, and treats pain and nausea per the Pain Management and Nausea-Vomiting Guidelines.

clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Intact in all extremities; less restless
otherFindings: Pain reduced to 5/10 approximately 5 minutes after hydromorphone
Nausea improved after ondansetron, no further emesis
Left costovertebral angle tenderness persists but patient is calmer
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "That's helping — it's not gone but I can breathe through it now."

expectedActions.shortAction: Assess pain using Numeric Rating Scale (patient >12 years old)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Greater than 12 years old: Self-report scale: Numeric Rating Scale (NRS)
expectedActions.rationale: Establishes a baseline pain score to measure response to treatment.

expectedActions.shortAction: Assess for life-threatening causes: AAA, ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, perforation
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Assess for life-threatening causes of abdominal pain, which may include: Signs and symptoms of dissecting or ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)
expectedActions.rationale: Flank/abdominal pain can mimic life-threatening pathology that must be ruled out before treating as simple renal colic.

expectedActions.shortAction: Establish IV access for analgesia administration
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Obtain vascular access as necessary to provide analgesia and/or fluid resuscitation
expectedActions.rationale: IV access is required for parenteral opioid and antiemetic administration.

expectedActions.shortAction: Hydromorphone 1 mg IV (70 kg × 0.015 mg/kg = 1.05 mg, rounded to 1 mg; max initial 2 mg, max cumulative 4 mg)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Hydromorphone: 0.015 mg/kg IM, IV, or IO (maximum initial dose 2 mg; maximum cumulative dose of 4 mg)
expectedActions.rationale: Weight-based opioid dosing for severe pain, capped below the protocol's maximum initial dose.

expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Ondansetron (contraindicated for suspected or known diagnosis of prolonged QT syndrome): Adult: 4 mg IV/PO/SL
expectedActions.rationale: Treats associated nausea and vomiting per the antiemetic guideline referenced from Pain Management.

expectedActions.shortAction: Place patient in position of comfort and reassess
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transport in position of comfort and reassess as indicated
expectedActions.rationale: Non-pharmacologic comfort measure that complements medication therapy.

transitions.if: Reassessed at 5 min, repeat dose given
transitions.condition: Pain remains at 5/10 five minutes after the initial dose; crew reassesses vital signs and pain score, confirms no hypotension or hypoventilation, and administers a repeat hydromorphone dose within the cumulative maximum.

Crew defers opioid administration out of concern for masking findings, despite the protocol explicitly noting analgesics do not delay diagnosis in acute abdominal pain; patient remains in severe uncontrolled pain.

phases.name: Reassessed at 5 min, repeat dose given
phases.description: Five minutes after the initial dose, pain remains moderate. Crew reassesses vital signs, confirms hemodynamic stability, and administers a repeat weight-based hydromorphone dose within the protocol's cumulative maximum before transporting.
phases.triggerCondition: Per protocol, pain medication may be repeated after 5 minutes if vital signs allow and pain persists; crew reassesses and administers a second dose within the cumulative maximum of 4 mg.

clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Intact in all extremities, resting comfortably on the stretcher
otherFindings: Pain reduced to 2/10 after repeat dose
Alert and cooperative, no respiratory depression
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Much better, thank you. That's tolerable now."

expectedActions.shortAction: Repeat hydromorphone 1 mg IV after 5 min (cumulative 2 mg; max cumulative 4 mg)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If indicated based on pain assessment, and vital signs allow, repeat pain medication administration (excluding acetaminophen and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicines) after 5 minutes of the previous dose
expectedActions.rationale: Repeat dosing follows the protocol's 5-minute reassessment interval and stays within the cumulative maximum.

expectedActions.shortAction: Monitor capnography/SpO2 for hypoventilation after repeat opioid dose
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Use of non-invasive capnography is an earlier predictor of hypoventilation than pulse oximetry if opioid medications are administered
expectedActions.rationale: Repeat opioid dosing increases cumulative respiratory depression risk requiring closer monitoring.

expectedActions.shortAction: Transport to appropriate receiving facility, reassess vitals en route
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Provide transport to an appropriate receiving facility. Reassess vital signs and response to therapeutic interventions throughout transport
expectedActions.rationale: Ensures continued monitoring and timely definitive care.

phases.name: Analgesia withheld despite protocol
phases.description: Crew withholds opioid analgesia out of concern for masking the clinical picture. The patient remains in severe, uncontrolled pain, continuing to writhe and becoming increasingly tachycardic and distressed.
phases.triggerCondition: Analgesia is deferred despite the protocol's explicit guidance that analgesic use for acute abdominal pain does not mask clinical findings or delay diagnosis; the patient's pain and distress escalate.

clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Intact; continues writhing, unable to remain still
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Please, it's not getting any better — can't you give me something?"

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize ongoing severe pain unresponsive to non-pharmacologic measures; administer hydromorphone
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patients with acute abdominal pain should receive analgesic interventions – Use of analgesics for acute abdominal pain does not mask clinical findings or delay diagnosis
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed recognition that opioid analgesia is indicated and safe for this presentation.
